Global Industrial Machinery Inc. - Q3 FY2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Global Industrial Machinery Inc. Q3 FY2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are in listen-only mode. After the presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. If you would like to register for a question, please press star then one on your telephone keypad. If you're using a speakerphone, please pick up your handset before pressing the keys. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Alex Rivera, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera (Vice President of Investor Relations):
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss Global Industrial Machinery Inc.'s, or GIMI's, results for the third quarter of fiscal year 2024. Joining me on today's call are Jonathan Hale, Chief Executive Officer; and Sarah Mitchell, Chief Financial Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we will be making today are forward-looking in nature and subject to certain risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Jonathan Hale.

Jonathan Hale (CEO):
Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report on GIMI's performance for Q3 FY2024. We've made significant progress on several fronts, navigating a complex macroeconomic environment while capitalizing on secular tailwinds in factory automation, electrification, and reshoring. One of our standout achievements was total order intake reaching $1.52 billion, up 18% year-over-year from $1.29 billion last year, marking our strongest quarterly bookings since the post-pandemic capex rebound and reflecting broad-based strength across discrete automation, process equipment, and heavy machinery segments. This drove our book-to-bill ratio to an impressive 1.28x, up from 0.92x a year ago and signaling robust backlog growth to a record $4.8 billion, providing over 14 months of revenue visibility.

Macroeconomic factors like elevated interest rates and supply chain pressures have tempered end-market demand in areas like automotive and construction, leading to a 7% overall decline in weighted demand metrics, but we've seen bright spots in semiconductors and aerospace, up 22% and 14% respectively, bolstered by CHIPS Act funding and defense backlogs. On revenue, we delivered solid organic growth of 8% in the quarter, complemented by inorganic contributions from our tuck-in acquisitions, pushing total revenue up 14% year-over-year.

We're confident that our strategic initiatives—in R&D for digital twins, AI-enabled platforms like Predix Edge, and modular designs—are positioning us for long-term sustainable growth, outpacing peers amid the industrial capex cycle inflection.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Sarah Mitchell to provide more detail on our financial results.

Sarah Mitchell (CFO):
Thank you, Jonathan. Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for joining our Q3 earnings call for Global Industrial Machinery Inc., or GIMI as many of you know us. As we dive into the financials, let's start with one of our most critical leading indicators: total order intake, which came in at $1.52 billion for the quarter, representing a robust 18% year-over-year growth from $1.29 billion in Q3 FY2023. This marks our strongest quarterly order intake since Q4 FY2021, when we benefited from the initial post-pandemic capex rebound.

To put this in context, our trailing 12-month order intake now stands at $5.9 billion, up 15% organically year-over-year, excluding minor FX headwinds from a stronger USD against the euro and yen. Our book-to-bill ratio expanded to 1.28x for the quarter—well above the 1.15x we saw in Q2—signaling strong visibility into FY2025 revenue as we convert this backlog. Ending backlog now sits at a record $4.8 billion, with approximately 65% expected to convert within the next 12 months.

Let me break this down by our key segments, where we saw broad-based strength driven by secular tailwinds like factory automation, reshoring initiatives, and the electrification megatrend. Discrete Automation, 45% of intake at $684 million, up 22% YoY, was the standout performer, fueled by hyperscaler data center builds and EV battery gigafactory ramps. We secured major wins, including a $150 million follow-on order from a leading U.S. OEM for our next-gen robotic palletizers integrated with AI vision systems—similar to what's powering Tesla's Gigafactory expansions. Our modular AGV platforms, with plug-and-play IoT connectivity for Industry 4.0, continue to displace legacy systems from competitors like Kuka and Fanuc.

Process Equipment, 30% of intake at $456 million, up 12% YoY, saw growth moderate slightly due to softer chemical capex amid high natural gas prices in Europe, but we offset this with strength in semiconductor backend tools. Notable was an $80 million order from a TSMC supplier for our high-precision wafer handling systems, leveraging our proprietary vacuum cluster architecture that's gaining share against Applied Materials' offerings.

Heavy Machinery & Aerospace, 25% of intake at $381 million, up 16% YoY, benefited from a sharp aerospace aftermarket rebound, with Boeing and Airbus ramping narrowbody production. We booked $60 million in turbine blade machining centers for a European primes supplier, benefiting from our investments in hybrid additive-subtractive CNC platforms that reduce lead times by 30% compared to traditional Haas or DMG Mori setups.

Regionally, the picture is encouragingly diversified: Americas at 42% of intake, up 25% YoY, propelled by U.S. reshoring under the CHIPS Act and IRA, with orders from Intel's Ohio fab and battery joint ventures like GM-Ultium, plus Mexico's nearshoring boom for auto tier-1s. EMEA at 28%, up 10% YoY, showed solid auto recovery in Germany, though energy transition delays in LNG equipment tempered growth—we're mitigating with our green steel forging presses aligned with EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism incentives. Asia-Pacific at 30%, up 15% YoY, faced lumpiness from China semi controls but shone through with offsets like a $45 million material handling order from Reliance Industries for their green energy parks, echoing Adani Group's expansions.

Strategically, this intake reflects the payoffs from our $250 million R&D reinvestment over the past 18 months in digital twin-enabled design and sustainable tech. Our Predix Edge AI suite, now embedded in 70% of new orders, delivers predictive maintenance that cuts customer downtime by 25%, driving repeat business and pricing power—up 4% average in Q3. We're also accelerating modularization to combat supply chain volatility; our standardized frame kits reduced custom engineering costs by 15% quarter-over-quarter.

Looking ahead, we see FY2024 order intake trending toward $5.9-6.1 billion, implying 13-16% growth, supported by a $2.6 billion pipeline of qualified opportunities. Risks include prolonged semi cyclicality and potential Eurozone slowdowns, but our 1.25x+ book-to-bill target and backlog provide a strong moat. We're well-positioned to outperform peers like Illinois Tool Works or Sandvik, who reported single-digit intake growth last quarter.

Today, I'd like to dive deep into our book-to-bill ratio and the trends underpinning it, as this remains a critical leading indicator for our visibility into future revenue streams in the industrial equipment sector. For those less familiar, our book-to-bill is calculated as quarterly bookings—firm customer orders—divided by quarterly billings, which are revenue recognized under ASC 606 from shipments and milestone completions. A ratio above 1.0 signals growing backlog and sustained demand momentum, which is especially vital in our cyclical industry where capex cycles in end-markets like automotive OEMs, aerospace, semiconductors, and renewables drive multi-quarter lead times.

In Q3, we delivered a book-to-bill ratio of 1.28, up sequentially from 1.15 in Q2 and markedly improved from 0.92 in Q3 last year. This marks our strongest quarterly reading since Q4 2022. Drilling down by segment: Automation & Robotics hit 1.45, fueled by hyperscaler demand for AI-enabled assembly lines. Bookings grew 32% quarter-over-quarter to $450 million, outpacing billings of $310 million. Think Fanuc-like collaborative robots integrated with our proprietary EdgeAI software for predictive maintenance—customers like Tesla and Foxconn are doubling down here.

Precision Machining & CNC at a robust 1.22, with $280 million in bookings versus $230 million billed. Aerospace OEMs, including Boeing and Airbus suppliers, are front-loading orders for titanium 5-axis mills amid supply chain derisking. Heavy Industrial Equipment steady at 1.10, reflecting mining and renewables exposure. Orders for our electric arc furnace melters—similar to those from SMS Group—rose 18% to $210 million, driven by steelmakers like Nucor pursuing green steel transitions.

Overall, Q3 bookings totaled $1.52 billion, a 28% sequential jump and 15% year-over-year growth, while billings came in at $1.19 billion. This pushed our backlog to that record $4.8 billion, up 22% from Q2 ends.

The sequential improvement reflects a classic inflection in the industrial capex cycle. After a soft H1 marked by high interest rates crimping OEM budgets, we're seeing reacceleration tied to three macro tailwinds: First, the AI and electrification boom—industrial automation bookings surged 40% YoY, mirroring SEMI's semiconductor book-to-bill hitting 1.5 in September—our fab equipment like wafer handling systems are riding that wave. Customers are investing in 'dark factories' with our IoT-connected CNCs for 24/7 throughput.

Second, regional dynamics: North America, 45% of bookings, book-to-bill at 1.35, bolstered by IRA incentives—US renewables orders for wind turbine gear reducers doubled, akin to Vestas' supply chain ramp. Asia-Pacific, 35%, exceptional 1.50 ratio, led by China's EV battery gigafactory builds—think CATL-scale orders for our lithium mixing equipment—and Taiwan's semi expansion. EMEA, 20%, recovering to 1.12 from 0.95 in Q2, as German auto OEMs like Volkswagen resume capex post-UAW strikes and Red Sea disruptions eased logistics.

Third, supply chain normalization—lead times compressed to 16 weeks from 24 in Q1, thanks to our $150 million in strategic inventory builds and dual-sourcing chips from TSMC and Samsung.

To sustain this momentum, we're leaning into Industry 4.0. Our 'Machinery-as-a-Service' model—now 15% of bookings—bundles our robots with subscription-based software updates, boosting recurring revenue to 12% of total, up from 8%. We've also launched Gen-3 digital twins for CNC simulation, reducing customer validation time by 30%, which has won us preferred supplier status at John Deere and Siemens.

Strategically, pricing remains firm at +4.5% YoY, supported by 75% backlog coverage for FY24. We're allocating $300 million from free cash flow to capacity expansion: a new 200,000 sq ft fab in Guadalajara, Mexico, for nearshoring, and automation upgrades at our Rockford, IL plant to lift output 25% by H2'25. Risks? Geopolitical tensions could pressure APAC semis, but our diversified end-markets—only 25% tied to autos—provide a buffer. Absent a recession, we see book-to-bill stabilizing at 1.20-1.30 into FY25, implying 12-15% organic growth.

Turning to our financial performance, GIMI reported $2.92 billion in revenue for the quarter, representing a 15% increase year-over-year. This strong blend reflects 8% organic growth for the quarter, excluding about 1% FX headwinds, complemented by a 7% inorganic lift from acquisitions—our strongest quarter of the year. Gross margin expanded to 43.2%, driven by favorable product mix in high-margin automation, pricing actions, and operational efficiencies from modular platforms. Operating expenses were $685 million, resulting in an operating income of $575 million. Our net income for the quarter was $420 million, or $2.15 per diluted share.

Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for joining us on the Global Industrial Dynamics earnings call—GIMI's platform. As we unpack this revenue performance, specifically the strong blend of organic growth and inorganic contributions from our disciplined M&A strategy. Full-year revenue to date positions us for $11.8 billion, a 13% increase. Excluding FX, this reflects 8% organic growth for Q3 and 7% year-to-date, complemented by 7% inorganic in the quarter and 5% annually from acquisitions.

Organic revenue growth, excluding acquisitions, divestitures, and FX, delivered 8% growth in Q3, driven by volume expansion, pricing discipline, and aftermarket services pull-through. Year-to-date organic growth of 7% marks our third consecutive year above 5%, outpacing the broader industrial equipment market, which grew mid-single digits per ISM indices.

By segment: Core Machinery, 52% of revenue, up 9% organically, fueled by 12% volume in high-margin CNC lathes and precision milling for semiconductor fab equipment and EV battery lines. ASPs rose 2% due to steel and aluminum passthroughs, with backlog at $4.8 billion, up 20% YoY. Automation & Robotics, 28%, organic growth of 10%, propelled by cobots and AI-enabled vision systems with EdgeControl PLCs—hyperscaler capex in data centers like NVIDIA and TSMC, and auto OEMs like Ford ramping flexible cells. Installed base grew 15%, driving 25% services attachment. Aftermarket & Services, 20%, a standout 6% organic increase, with uptime contracts via Dynapredict IoT yielding 85% renewals—this annuity now 22% of total revenue, up from 19%.

Regionally balanced but APAC-led: Americas, 45%, 7% growth with CHIPS Act and IRA boosting modular lines from Intel and GM Ultium. EMEA, 30%, 6% amid softer German autos, offset by Vestas wind OEMs adopting gearless drivetrains. APAC, 25%, 12% surge from China's 'Made in China 2025' and India's PLI for electronics, with frame agreements at Foxconn and Tata.

Key enablers: $250 million FY2024 R&D—8% of sales—in digital twins and ML for adaptive manufacturing. VulcanForge reduced setup times by 30%, shifting mix to premium products.

Inorganic contributions added $204 million or 7% to Q3 revenue: Q2's RoboFlex GmbH (Germany, $180M) contributed with fiber laser welders, $25M synergies via cross-selling to NA autos. Q3's Precision Dynamics Inc. (U.S., $220M) added servo motors for semi etch tools, 20% cost savings via shared supply chain. Q4 bolt-on AsiaTech Automation (Singapore, $150M) kicked in cleanroom robotics for Samsung OLED, enhancing APAC with $15M FY2025 synergies.

Pro forma, accretive to EBITDA margins by 50 bps year one, ROIC above 12% by year two. Pipeline at $1.5 billion for software-embedded hardware.

We continue to maintain a strong balance sheet, with $1.3 billion in cash and cash equivalents, 2.0x net debt to EBITDA. We are committed to investing in our business to drive future growth and shareholder value, guiding FY2024 organic growth of 7-9%, mid-teens total revenue, 18%+ adjusted EBITDA margins.

Now, I'd like to dive deep into the impact of macroeconomic factors on our end market demand, as this has been the most frequently cited question. Our team has been laser-focused on navigating this volatile landscape.

First, the macro stage: Persistent high interest rates at 5.25-5.50% have crimped capex budgets. ISM Manufacturing PMI at 48.7 signals contraction, with inflation at 2.4% CPI but sticky input costs up 8-12%. Geopolitics inflated freight 25-30% YoY.

These translated to a 7% YoY decline in end market demand, book-to-bill to 0.92x average but recovering, backlog $4.8 billion up 2% sequentially.

By end market: Automotive, 28% revenue, softened 12% YoY on high inventory (2.8M units) and EV chop—TSMC/Tesla ramps but GM/Ford delays. 'EV Forge' secured $150M, auto book-to-bill 1.05x.

Aerospace & defense, 22%, bright 14% growth on Boeing/Airbus backlogs (17K orders), though strikes delayed 5%. DoD FY2025 up 4.1% to $886B fuels MRO. NA 18%, EMEA 9%.

Semiconductor equipment, 15%, surged 22% on CHIPS $52B—TSMC Arizona needs $200M+ AS/RS. 95% utilization, APAC 60% growth despite China 75% utilization.

Construction/mining, 18%, steepest 15% drop on 8% construction starts, 6.5% mortgage rates, copper volatility. CrawlerPro upticks from Rio Tinto. EMEA down 20% on energy crisis.

General industrial, 17%, down 6% on 77.5% utilization, but cobots up 25% on labor shortages.

Regionally: NA 55% revenue, -1% buoyed by reshoring, 15% share in Ohio assembly. APAC 30% down 10% on China PMI 49.8. EMEA 15% -14% on gas prices/autos.

We're accelerating: 'Resilient Edge' $250M in AI predictive maintenance, cutting downtime 30%, 12% CAGR service annuities. 40% Q3 orders low-emission hydraulics for EU Stage V. Inventory to 14 weeks, protecting 55% gross margins? Wait, 43% as stated.

Forward: Q4 stabilizing with rate cuts, 3-5% uptick if 10Y to 3.8%. Risks: elections, tariffs shave 2-3% APAC. With $1.3B cash, 2.0x debt/EBITDA, 18% ROIC target, built for cycle.

Operator, that concludes my prepared remarks. We'd now be happy to take your questions.

Q&A Session:

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question-and-answer session. Our first question comes from Ben Thompson with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Ben Thompson (JPMorgan):
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the demand environment you're seeing in the automation market?

Jonathan Hale (CEO):
Good morning, Ben. Absolutely, the automation market remains a key growth driver for us. As Sarah detailed, discrete automation orders jumped 22% YoY to $684 million, driven by hyperscalers building data centers and EV gigafactories. We've seen major wins like the $150 million robotic palletizer order, leveraging AI vision and modular AGVs that integrate seamlessly into Industry 4.0 setups, displacing incumbents. Despite macro headwinds like high rates slowing some OEM capex, AI tailwinds and reshoring are accelerating, with our Predix Edge AI now in 70% of orders boosting predictive maintenance and repeat buys. Regionally, Americas and APAC are leading, and we expect this segment to sustain 20%+ growth into FY2025 as 'dark factories' proliferate.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Lisa Chen with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Lisa Chen (Goldman Sachs):
What are your expectations for capital expenditures in the coming year?

Sarah Mitchell (CFO):
Thanks, Lisa. For FY2025, we're guiding capex to $350-400 million, up modestly from $320 million this year, focused on high-ROI capacity expansions. This includes the new 200,000 sq ft Guadalajara fab for nearshoring, automation upgrades at Rockford to boost output 25% by H2'25, and further R&D in digital twins and Gen-3 CNC sims. About 60% ties to organic growth levers like modularization and MaaS scaling to 20% of bookings, with the rest supporting acquisition integrations like AsiaTech's cleanroom robotics. This keeps us at 3-4% of revenue, preserving free cash flow conversion above 90% while targeting 18%+ ROIC. We're funding from operations, maintaining our $1.3 billion cash fortress.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Mike Patel with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Mike Patel (Morgan Stanley):
How are you managing supply chain disruptions, and what impact are they having on your margins?

Jonathan Hale (CEO):
Mike, supply chain management is a top priority, and we've made great strides. Lead times are down to 16 weeks from 24 earlier this year via $150 million strategic inventory, dual-sourcing chips from TSMC/Samsung, and standardized frame kits cutting custom engineering 15% QoQ. Red Sea and geopolitics raised freight 25-30%, but nearshoring to Mexico and Ohio assembly mitigates this—Guadalajara fab online soon. Margins held firm at 43.2% gross, up 120 bps YoY, from automation mix, 4.5% pricing, and efficiencies; services annuities now 22% of revenue at high margins. Minor input cost passthroughs on steel/aluminum, but our diversified suppliers buffer semi cyclicality. Overall, no material margin erosion expected.

Closing Remarks:

Jonathan Hale (CEO):
Thank you for your questions and your interest in GIMI. We are pleased with our progress this quarter—record backlog, strong book-to-bill, resilient demand pockets amid macros—and remain focused on executing our strategy around digitalization, electrification, and M&A to deliver long-term value for our shareholders.

Alex Rivera (Vice President of Investor Relations):
Thank you, everyone, for joining us today. This concludes our earnings call. Have a great day.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
